part.title: Safety talk for new trampers

turns.text: Kia ora everyone, and welcome along. I'm Dougal Fraser, and I've been leading trips for the Canterbury Ridge Tramping Club for about twelve years now. Tonight's all about staying safe out in the hills, so grab a cuppa and get comfy.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: First, a quick word about your first trip with us. Normally we'd take new members up to Arthur's Pass, but there are roadworks on the highway all month, so that's off. We do evening walks on the Port Hills, but those are for people who've already been out with us. So your first one will be over on Banks Peninsula, on Saturday the twenty-third.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Right, planning. When people plan a tramp, they tend to spend ages on how hard the track's graded, or on sorting out who's driving. Both matter, sure. But the one thing I insist on, above everything else, is that you leave details of your route and the time you expect to be out by. No exceptions.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Now, who do you leave those details with? Years ago we used to drop a form in at the Department of Conservation visitor centre, but they stopped accepting them a while back. And please don't send it to our club secretary, because she can't be by the phone around the clock. Give it to a friend or someone in your family, someone you trust to raise the alarm if you're not back.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Okay, equipment, starting with your feet. The club has a few rain jackets members can borrow, but we haven't got any boots, sorry. And I'm not going to inspect everyone's footwear at the car park either. What I will ask is that you don't turn up in boots straight out of the box. Wear them around town for a couple of weeks first, so they're properly broken in.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Next, the weather, which in this part of the country can change in minutes. Lots of you will just check the weather app on your phone. The club website does post a forecast link too, but it's often a day out of date. The one we rely on is the mountain forecast on MetService, because it's specific to the high country.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: So what happens if the weather turns on us halfway through a trip? Most people assume we'd just turn round and go back the way we came. Actually, that's often not the safest choice, because you'd be heading back over exposed ridges. Sitting it out and waiting isn't great either, as you get cold really fast. What we normally do is drop down to a lower track, an escape route we'll have worked out in advance.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: And rivers. Crossings are one of the biggest risks for trampers in this country. Our rule used to be that you didn't cross if the water was above waist height, but that's far too deep when it's flowing fast. So now it's simple: if it's higher than your knees, nobody goes in. People ask whether linking arms makes it okay, and it helps, but it doesn't change the rule.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Right, let's talk about what goes in your pack. The club carries a personal locator beacon and the main first-aid kit, and the trip leader looks after both, so you don't need your own.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: But every single person must bring a head torch, even on a day walk, because delays happen. You'll also need a spare warm layer, like a fleece, however sunny it looks when you set off. A paper map's handy, but I'll always have one, so that's up to you.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Now, emergencies. If someone gets hurt, don't move them unless they're in danger where they are. And don't give them anything to eat or drink yet, until we know how bad it is. What you should do is get something underneath them and keep them warm, because the cold's the real danger out there. Then, if it's serious, we set off the beacon, which sends our exact position to the rescue services.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: In the old days, you'd send one person running out to get help. We don't do that any more. We keep the group together, and nobody heads off on their own.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Last thing: next Thursday's session. We'd hoped to have a volunteer from LandSAR, the search and rescue people, but they can't come till next month. So instead we'll head out onto the field behind the hall for some map and compass practice. And I'll give you a proper demonstration of how the beacon works, since any of you might need to set it off one day.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.say: The first-aid course is separate, by the way. That's a weekend in March, and it costs eighty-five dollars. And no, sorry, there's no gear sale this year. Right, any questions?

Right, let's talk about what goes in your pack. The club carries a personal locator beacon and the main first aid kit, and the trip leader looks after both, so you don't need your own.

But every single person must bring a head torch, even on a day walk, because delays happen. You'll also need a spare warm layer, like a fleece, however sunny it looks when you set off. A paper map's handy, but I'll always have one, so that's up to you.

Now, emergencies: if someone gets hurt, don't move them unless they're in danger where they are, and don't give them anything to eat or drink yet until we know how bad it is. What you should do is get something underneath them and keep them warm, because the cold's the real danger out there. Then, if it's serious, we set off the beacon, which sends our exact position to the rescue services.
In the old days, you'd send one person running out to get help. We don't do that anymore. We keep the group together and nobody heads off on their own.

Last thing, next Thursday's session. We'd hoped to have a volunteer from LANSAR, the search and rescue people, but they can't come till next month. So, instead, we'll head out onto the field behind the hall for some map and compass practice, and I'll give you a proper demonstration of how the beacon works, since any of you might need to set it off one day.
The first aid course is separate, by the way. That's a weekend in March and it costs eighty-five dollars. And no, sorry, there's no gear sale this year. Right, any questions?
